title: Hold the matrix operation fixed.
lead: Compare algorithms for the same four-by-four FP32 inputs.
captions: Chapter Fourteen investigates one matrix multiplication. Keep the inputs, dimensions, number format and final output fixed while changing how input values are reused.
The baseline computes sixteen outputs separately. Its teaching algorithm explicitly loads one hundred and twenty-eight input values and stores sixteen results.

title: Share input tiles without changing the result.
lead: Tile widths two and four reduce explicit input loads.
captions: A tile width of two shares loaded inputs across several outputs and reduces the count to sixty-four input loads. A width of four reduces it to thirty-two.
Every choice produces the same complete output matrix in this model. These are explicit algorithm loads with cache reuse excluded; they are not measured physical memory traffic.

title: Larger tiles also consume block resources.
lead: Fewer loads do not establish the fastest implementation.
captions: With the chapter’s synthetic resource budgets, tile width two uses thirty-two shared-memory bytes and two hundred and fifty-six registers per block. Four blocks fit those budgets.

Tile width four uses one hundred and twenty-eight shared-memory bytes and one thousand and twenty-four registers per block. Only one block fits. This capacity bound is not a schedule or a timing measurement.

title: Write a hypothesis and its uncertainty.
lead: Choose what to investigate, then name the missing evidence.
captions: A useful recommendation states both the benefit and the cost. A larger tile reduces explicit input loads while using more registers and shared memory per block.
Either tile can be a hypothesis worth investigating. Neither a lower load count nor a higher block capacity proves which implementation is faster on a physical GPU.

title: Pause: double the matrix dimension.
lead: Use eight-by-eight inputs and tile width two.
captions: Now use eight-by-eight inputs with tile width two and the same resource budgets. Predict input loads, output stores and resident-block capacity.
Does doubling the matrix dimension double every count? Separate complete-operation counts from resources needed by one block before comparing the answer.

title: Different counts grow at different rates.
lead: The per-block resource requirement stays the same.
captions: This eight-by-eight case loads five hundred and twelve input values and stores sixty-four outputs. Four blocks still fit the stated teaching budgets.
At fixed tile width, input loads grow with the cube of the matrix dimension, while output stores grow with its square. The resources used by one block do not change here.

title: Measure equivalent implementations fairly.
lead: Check results, define the timed interval, then repeat.
captions: To compare real implementations, first check both outputs against a suitable reference. Keep inputs and number format comparable, and change one proposed optimisation at a time.
Define whether timing includes allocation and transfers. Warm up, wait for the GPU work in the chosen interval, repeat measurements, and inspect actual operations with a profiler.

title: Turn the model into a testable recommendation.
lead: Record evidence, assumptions and the next experiment.
captions: The browser supports a reuse argument and a resource trade-off. It does not identify the fastest kernel or measure physical GPU performance.
Return to Chapter Fourteen and write your recommendation: which tile would you test first, what evidence supports it, what uncertainty remains, and what measurement would resolve it?
